mainTopic: How far a wife's report, or one witness, is trusted about a husband's death in war, fire, or at sea.
overview: This amud asks how far we trust a report that a husband died when the danger was war, fire, or the sea. First the גמרא finishes asking whether a woman who says 'there was war and my husband died' is believed because of מה לי לשקר, or whether we worry she is only guessing (בדדמי). Two ברייתות are brought as proof, a smoke-filled house or cave and an attack by bandits, and each is pushed aside with its own special reason. Next comes a story of a fire at a wedding, where the wife cried 'Look at my husband!' and a burnt body and a hand were found. רב חייא בר אבין compares it to the smoke case, and רבא disagrees. The גמרא then shows how רב חייא בר אבין explains away the evidence. Then a new question opens: is one witness believed about a death in war? The story of נחמיה איש בית דלי is turned away by רבא's reading. The story of a sunken ship is also rejected, because the women must have seen the bodies brought up, and that discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The two sides of the question: believe her, or worry she is guessing?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes laying out its question. One side says she is believed because she could have said 'there was peace.' The other side says that once war is accepted, she may just be guessing that her husband died.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because if she wanted to lie, she could have said, 'There was peace in the world.' Or perhaps, once the war is accepted, she is saying what she imagines happened. Then the argument 'Why would I lie?' does not come and weaken the accepted fact that there was a war.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a question it started just before this section. A woman says there was a war and her husband died, and the גמרא asks whether we believe her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one: she could have left out the war and just said 'he died in peacetime,' so mentioning the war is not a trick. That is a מה לי לשקר, and it makes her believable. Side two: once there is a war in the picture, people easily assume the worst and say what they guess (בדדמי). Her מה לי לשקר cannot erase the fact that a war is now accepted.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Why would I lie?' She could have made a better claim, so we trust the one she made.
Based on what seems likely; speaking from a guess, not from certain knowledge.
It became established or accepted (here, that there was a war).
'Or perhaps.' This introduces the other side of a question.

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not whether she is lying on purpose. Side two says she may honestly believe he died, but she is only assuming it, because in a war people expect the worst.

phrases.english: Because if she wanted, she could have said:
'There was peace in the world.'
Or perhaps: since it has become established (that there was war),
she says what she imagines happened,
and 'why would I lie' does not come
and weaken its established status.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a question that began before this section.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does מה לי לשקר make her believable when she herself reports a war, or does the war make her testimony a mere guess (בדדמי)?

steps.title: Proof attempt: the smoke-filled house or cave
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: if she says they smoked out our house or cave, he died and I was saved, she is not believed. This looks like proof that her own report of danger does not help her.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'They filled our house with smoke,' or 'They filled our cave with smoke,' and 'He died and I was saved.' She is not believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer the question from a ברייתא about a fire or smoke attack.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here she herself told us about the danger, just like the war case. She still is not believed. That seems to show that מה לי לשקר does not help, and we worry that she is only guessing.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Come and hear.' This introduces a source brought as a proof.
They filled with smoke (they set on fire).

phrases.english: Come and hear:
'They filled our house with smoke on us,'
'They filled our cave with smoke on us,'
'He died, and I was saved' —
she is not believed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to settle the question from Step 1.
steps.raayaObject: The second side of the question: her own report of danger does not make her believable.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a house or cave filled with smoke.

steps.title: Rejected: in a fire, he may have been saved by a miracle too
steps.stepSummary: The fire case is different. We tell her: just as a miracle saved you, a miracle may have saved him.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because we say to her: just as a miracle happened for you, a miracle also happened for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof. The fire case has its own reason for not believing her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a fire or smoke attack, everyone inside was in the same danger. If she escaped, he could have escaped too. So she is not believed for that reason, not because מה לי לשקר fails. The question stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is different there.' This shows the case is not comparable.

phrases.english: It is different there, because one says to her:
just as a miracle happened for you,
a miracle also happened for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in Step 2.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof from the fire case. The question itself is untouched.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: In a fire, both were in equal danger, so her survival suggests he might also have survived. That is a separate reason not to believe her.

steps.title: Second proof attempt: attacked by גוים or bandits
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא: if she says גוים or bandits attacked us, he died and I was saved, she is believed. This looks like proof that מה לי לשקר works.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'גוים attacked us,' or 'Bandits attacked us,' and 'He died and I was saved.' She is believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries again, now from a case where she is believed even though she reported the danger herself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the war case, she told us about the danger and still is believed. It seems the reason is מה לי לשקר, which would support side one of the question.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
'Gentiles attacked us,'
'Bandits attacked us,'
'He died, and I was saved' — she is believed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof failed, this tries a new proof for the opposite side.
steps.raayaObject: The first side of the question: she is believed because of מה לי לשקר.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about an attack by גוים or bandits.

steps.title: Rejected: a woman's 'weapons' protect her, as רב אידי taught
steps.stepSummary: She is believed there for a different reason, following רב אידי: attackers usually do not kill a woman. That explains why she survived and he did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: There it follows רב אידי, as רב אידי said: a woman, her weapons are upon her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the second proof by giving another reason she is believed in the bandit case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Attackers usually kill the men but not the women; being a woman is her 'protection.' So it makes sense that she lived and he died, and her story is believable on its own terms. The case proves nothing about מה לי לשקר, so the question remains open.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא whose saying explains this case.
In line with the view of רב (so-and-so).

steps.whatToRemember: Both proofs were turned away. In the fire case she is not believed because he could have survived just like her. In the bandit case she is believed because attackers spare women. Neither case settles whether מה לי לשקר helps when she herself reports a war.

phrases.english: There, it is in line with רב אידי.
For רב אידי said:
A woman, her weapons are upon her.
phrases.notes: He means being a woman protects her, because attackers usually don't kill women.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in Step 4.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof from the bandit case.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: She is believed there because her survival makes sense (women are not usually killed), not because of מה לי לשקר.

steps.title: A story: fire breaks out at the end of a wedding
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a story. At the end of a man's wedding, his canopy caught fire. His wife cried out 'Look at my husband!' and people found a burnt man and a palm of a hand lying there.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man: at the end of his wedding, a fire broke out in his bridal canopy. His wife said to them, 'Look at my husband! Look at my husband!' They came and saw a burnt man lying there, and a palm of a hand lying there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts telling a real case about a woman saying her husband died in a fire. This sets up the discussion that follows: רב חייא בר אבין's view in the next step and רבא's reply after it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This connects to the smoke-and-fire ברייתא in Step 2, where she is not believed, for the reason given in Step 3. Here people actually saw a burnt body and a hand, but it is not clear the body can be identified as her husband. The ruling on this case comes next.

phrases.english: A certain man, at the end of whose wedding
a fire broke out in his bridal canopy.
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the corrected wording is the one in square brackets, meaning 'his canopy.'

phrases.english: His wife said to them:
'Look at my husband! Look at my husband!'
They came and saw a burnt man lying there,
and the palm of a hand lying there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the theoretical question to a real-life case of a husband said to have died in a fire.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling yet. The story sets up a case about a wife's report and a burnt body whose identity is unclear.

steps.title: רב חייא בר אבין compares the canopy fire to the smoke case
steps.stepSummary: רב חייא בר אבין wants to say the burning-canopy case is the same as the smoke case, where the wife is not believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חייא בר אבין thought: this is just like the case of 'they smoked out our house' or 'they smoked out our cave' (where she is not believed).
steps.whatsHappening: רב חייא בר אבין gives his view on the canopy story: it matches the smoke ברייתא, so the wife should not be believed. This sets up רבא's reply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the smoke case (step 2), she is not believed because a miracle that saved her could also have saved him. A fire at the חופה looks like the same kind of case, so רב חייא בר אבין treats her the same way.

keyTerms.meaning: He thought to say (a first idea that may be challenged)

phrases.aramaic: סָבַר רַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָבִין לְמֵימַר:
phrases.english: Rav Chiyya bar Avin thought to say:
This is the case of "They smoked out the house on us,
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא from step 2, where she is not believed.

phrases.english: they smoked out the cave on us."

steps.triggerLanguage: סָבַר רַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָבִין לְמֵימַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a ruling on the story begun in step 6 by comparing it to the smoke ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The canopy-fire case is like the smoke case, so the wife is not believed.

steps.title: רבא: the canopy case is not like the smoke case
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects the comparison. Here she cried out right away, and there is real physical evidence: a burnt man and a hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Are these cases really alike? In the smoke case she did not cry out 'Look at my husband!' Also, here there is a burnt man lying there and a palm of a hand lying there.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes back on רב חייא בר אבין and gives two differences between the cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Difference one: here she shouted 'look at my husband' at the moment it happened, not as a story told later. Difference two: here her words are backed by evidence, a burnt body and a hand. So the reason from the smoke case (maybe he was also saved by a miracle) seems weaker here.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it comparable? (a way of rejecting a comparison)

phrases.english: Rava said: Are they comparable?
There she did not say
"Look at my husband, look at my husband."
And furthermore, there is a burnt man who lies there,
and a palm of a hand that lies there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the comparison made in step 7.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The comparison between the canopy fire and the smoke case.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The smoke case had no shout at the moment it happened and no physical evidence. The canopy case has both.

steps.title: How רב חייא בר אבין explains away the evidence
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why רב חייא בר אבין is not convinced. The burnt man could be someone else, and the husband could have lost his hand and run away in shame.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב חייא בר אבין? The burnt man lying there: say another person came to rescue him and the fire burned that person. The hand lying there: the fire burned the husband and left him with a blemish, and out of embarrassment he went and ran away somewhere.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב חייא בר אבין by showing that the evidence רבא pointed to does not prove the husband died.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each piece of evidence has another explanation. The burnt body may belong to a rescuer. The cut-off hand may be the husband's, but losing a hand does not mean he died. He may be alive and hiding out of shame.

phrases.english: And Rav Chiyya bar Avin?
phrases.notes: The גמרא is asking how he would answer רבא's two points.

phrases.english: The burnt man who lies there:
say another person came to rescue,
and the fire consumed him.
And the palm of the hand that lies there:
the fire burned him and a blemish formed on him,
and because of embarrassment
he went and ran away to the world.
phrases.notes: "To the world" means somewhere far away. He is still alive.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's evidence from step 8 on behalf of רב חייא בר אבין.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives another way to explain the evidence
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The burnt man and the hand prove the husband died.
steps.terutzMaskana: The evidence can be explained without the husband dying, so רב חייא בר אבין still does not trust her.
steps.whatToRemember: רב חייא בר אבין: not believed (like the smoke case). רבא: believed, because she shouted at once and there is evidence. רב חייא בר אבין's answer: the evidence does not prove death.

steps.title: Is one witness believed about a death in war?
steps.stepSummary: A new question: is one witness believed when he says the husband died in a war? It depends on why one witness is believed in the first place.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: what about one witness who says the husband died in war? The reason one witness is believed is that the truth is likely to come out, so he won't lie. If so, here too he won't lie. Or maybe the reason is that she herself checks carefully before she remarries. Here, since sometimes she hates him, she won't check carefully before marrying.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question and lays out two possible reasons for trusting one witness. Each reason leads to a different answer for war.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Reason 1: a witness will not tell a lie that is likely to be found out (if the husband is alive, he will show up). That holds in war too, so he is believed. Reason 2: we rely on the wife to check carefully before remarrying. If she sometimes hates her husband, she may not check carefully in the confusion of war, so the witness is not enough.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked before them
A matter that is likely to come out
She checks carefully and then marries

phrases.english: It was asked of them:
One witness in a war, what is the law?
The reason one witness is believed
is because it is a matter that is likely to be revealed,
so he does not lie;
here too he does not lie.
Or perhaps: the reason for one witness
is because she herself checks carefully and then marries,
and here, since sometimes she hates him,
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets are added in the corrected wording.

phrases.english: she does not check carefully and marries.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic. It moves from the wife's own word to one witness in wartime.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is one witness believed about a husband's death in war? It depends on whether he is trusted because a lie would come out, or because the wife checks carefully.
steps.confusionAlert: The question is not whether the witness is honest in general. It is about which reason makes one witness enough, and whether that reason still works in war.

steps.title: רמי בר חמא: רבי עקיבא's story about troops
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא brings a story. נחמיה איש בית דלי told רבי עקיבא a tradition from רבן גמליאל הזקן that a woman may remarry on one witness, in a land full of troops.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא said: Come hear. רבי עקיבא said: When I went down to נהרדעא to make the year a leap year, נחמיה איש בית דלי met me. He said: I heard that in ארץ ישראל they don't let a woman remarry on one witness, except רבי יהודה בן בבא. I said: That's right. He said: Tell them in my name: you know this land is overrun with troops? I have a tradition from רבן גמליאל הזקן that a woman may remarry on one witness.
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר חמא tries to answer the question about one witness in war with a story about רבי עקיבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נחמיה stresses that the land is full of troops, which is close to war. Even so, he passes on רבן גמליאל הזקן's tradition that one witness is enough. That seems to show one witness is believed even in war-like conditions.

keyTerms.meaning: To make the year a leap year

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא: תָּא שְׁמַע,
phrases.english: Rami bar Chama said: Come and hear,
Rabbi Akiva said:
When I went down to Neharde'a to make the year a leap year,
Nechemya of Beit D'li found me,
and said to me: I heard

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין מַשִּׂיאִין אֶת הָאִשָּׁה בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
phrases.english: that they do not let a woman remarry in Eretz Yisrael
based on one witness,
except Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava.
And I said to him: That is so.
He said to me: Tell them in my name:

phrases.aramaic: אַתֶּם יוֹדְעִים הַמְּדִינָה הַזּוֹ מְשׁוּבֶּשֶׁת בִּגְיָיסוֹת?
phrases.english: Do you know that this country is overrun with troops?
This is what I received from Rabban Gamliel the Elder:

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁמַּשִּׂיאִין הָאִשָּׁה עַל פִּי עֵד אֶחָד.
phrases.english: that they let a woman remarry based on one witness.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא: תָּא שְׁמַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question raised in step 10.
steps.raayaObject: Is one witness believed about a death in war?
steps.raayaSupportSource: נחמיה איש בית דלי's tradition from רבן גמליאל הזקן, said about a land full of troops: a woman may remarry on one witness.
steps.whyThisMatters: If this proof holds, one witness would be enough even in war-like conditions, which matches the first reason in step 10.

steps.title: Reading the story as proof that one witness is believed in wartime
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why the story of נחמיה איש בית דלי seems to prove that one עד אחד is believed even in a war zone.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'a land full of troops' mean? It must mean: even though this land is full of troops, I have a tradition that a woman may remarry based on one witness. So one witness is believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the proof that רמי בר חמא started in Step 11. It explains how the words 'a land full of troops' fit the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'full of troops' are read as 'even though.' Even in a war zone, where people die in confusing ways, one witness is enough. That would answer the question from Step 10 with a yes.

keyTerms.meaning: A land in turmoil, full of danger
We allow a woman to remarry

phrases.english: What is the point of 'a land full of troops'?

phrases.aramaic: לָאו, אַף עַל גַּב דִּמְדִינָה זוֹ מְשׁוּבֶּשֶׁת,
phrases.english: Doesn't it mean: even though this land is full of troops,
this is the tradition I received:
that we let a woman remarry based on one witness.
So we see that one witness is believed.
phrases.notes: He means believed even in a war situation, which was the question in Step 10.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the story quoted in Step 11.
steps.raayaObject: Whether one witness is believed that the husband died in a war.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The tradition of נחמיה איש בית דלי from רבן גמליאל, read as 'even though the land is full of troops.'

steps.title: רבא asks why he said 'this land' and not 'any place'
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges the reading: if this were a rule about war zones, he would have said 'any place with troops.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: If so, why say 'this land'? He should have said 'any place where there are troops'!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks the way the story was just read. His question sets up his own new reading in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A general rule about war would be worded in a general way. Saying 'this land' points to something about this specific place. So the troops are probably not part of the law at all.

phrases.english: רבא said: If so,
why did he say 'this land' in particular?
He should have said 'any place where there are troops'!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: אִי הָכִי, מַאי שְׁנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reading given in Step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that 'full of troops' means 'even in a war zone.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A general war rule would say 'any place with troops,' not 'this land.'

steps.title: רבא's reading: the troops only explain why he couldn't come in person
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that the troops were his reason for sending the message instead of coming to the Rabbis. So the story proves nothing about wartime testimony.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said, this is what he meant: You know this land is full of troops, and I cannot leave my family and come before the Rabbis. So I am telling you this way: I have a tradition from רבן גמליאל that a woman may remarry based on one witness.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a new reading of the story. The mention of troops is just his excuse for not traveling, so the proof from Step 12 falls away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this reading, the troops have nothing to do with the law. The tradition is the regular rule that one witness is believed. It says nothing about a death in war, so the question from Step 10 is still open.

keyTerms.meaning: I have a tradition, I received

steps.whatToRemember: The story of נחמיה איש בית דלי does not prove anything about war. 'This land is full of troops' only explains why he couldn't come in person.

phrases.english: Rather, רבא said, this is what he meant:

phrases.aramaic: אַתֶּם יוֹדְעִים שֶׁמְּדִינָה זוֹ מְשׁוּבֶּשֶׁת בִּגְיָיסוֹת,
phrases.english: You know that this land is full of troops,

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא אֶפְשָׁר לִי לְמִשְׁבַּק אִינָשֵׁי בֵיתִי
phrases.english: and I cannot leave the people of my household
and come before the Rabbis.
This is the tradition I received from רבן גמליאל:

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁמַּשִּׂיאִין הָאִשָּׁה עַל פִּי עֵד אֶחָד.
phrases.english: that we let a woman remarry based on one witness.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's own question from Step 13 with a new reading that cancels the proof from Step 12.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the story of נחמיה איש בית דלי.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The troops explain why he couldn't come in person. They are not part of the law, so the story says nothing about war.

steps.title: Proof from the sunken ship where רבי relied on women
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a story where רבי let the wives of drowned scholars remarry based on women's testimony. Water is like war, and many women count as one witness, so one witness should be believed in war.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: Two Torah scholars were traveling on a ship with אבא יוסי בן סימאי, and it sank. רבי let their wives remarry based on the testimony of women. But water is like war, and women, even a hundred of them, count like one witness. And still it says he let them remarry!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a second proof for the question from Step 10. It uses a sea disaster as a stand-in for war.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Drowning, like war, leaves room for guessing and mistakes. Women's testimony here counts like one witness. If רבי accepted it in a sea disaster, one witness should also be believed about a death in war.

phrases.aramaic: תָּא שְׁמַע: מַעֲשֶׂה בִּשְׁנֵי תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים
phrases.english: Come and hear: There was a story with two Torah scholars

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהָיוּ בָּאִין עִם אַבָּא יוֹסֵי בֶּן סִימַאי בִּסְפִינָה,
phrases.english: who were traveling on a ship with אבא יוסי בן סימאי,
and it sank, and רבי let their wives remarry

But water is like war.

phrases.aramaic: וְנָשִׁים, אֲפִילּוּ מֵאָה — כְּעֵד אֶחָד דָּמוּ,
phrases.english: And women, even a hundred of them, count like one witness,
and yet it teaches: he let them remarry!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: מַעֲשֶׂה בִּשְׁנֵי תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof fell away in Step 14, the גמרא tries a new proof for the same question.
steps.raayaObject: Whether one witness is believed that the husband died in a war.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about רבי allowing remarriage after a shipwreck based on women's testimony.

steps.title: The ship case must mean the women saw the bodies
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. A ship that sank in מים שאין להם סוף would not allow the wives to remarry at all, so the women must have said the bodies were brought up in front of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can you really think that? This is endless water, and with endless water the wife is forbidden. Rather, what is the case? The women said: they were brought up in front of us.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the shipwreck proof. It shows the women must have testified about something stronger than just seeing the ship sink.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the women only saw the ship go down in endless water, no number of witnesses would help, since the man may have reached a far shore. So the women must have seen the bodies pulled out. That kind of testimony leaves no room for guessing, so it is not like war.

keyTerms.meaning: And can you really think so?
Water with no visible end, where the shore cannot be seen all around
They were brought up in front of us

steps.confusionAlert: The problem with מים שאין להם סוף is not that the women are weak witnesses. Even seeing the ship sink does not prove the man died, because he could have come out somewhere out of sight.

phrases.aramaic: וְתִסְבְּרָא? מַיִם שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם סוֹף נִינְהוּ,
phrases.english: Can you really think that? This is endless water,

phrases.aramaic: וּמַיִם שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם סוֹף — אִשְׁתּוֹ אֲסוּרָה.
phrases.english: and when a man falls into endless water, his wife is forbidden to remarry.
Rather, what is the case?
The women said: they were brought up in front of us
phrases.notes: They mean the drowned men were pulled out of the water while the women watched.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתִסְבְּרָא? מַיִם שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם סוֹף נִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from Step 15 by changing what the women must have testified.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the shipwreck story.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A sinking in endless water can't permit remarriage by itself, so the women must have seen the bodies. That makes the case unlike a doubtful war death.
